file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Glob
tools.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

schema.name: Glob
schema.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

schema.name: Grep
schema.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]

When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

1	# Product
2	
3	## Register
4	
5	brand
6	
7	## Users
8	
9	Founders, developers and docs leads who have never heard of FirstRun. They land on the homepage cold, often from a link in a post. They read for about 10 seconds before they decide whether to stay. They are technical, but they are not here to read logs, traces or a financial model.
10	
11	## Product Purpose
12	
13	FirstRun checks documentation by running it. Two tools:
14	
15	- **Doc-test** runs a quickstart in a clean container, finds the first step that breaks, fixes the docs and proves the fix in a second clean run. This is the main action. A visitor should paste a docs URL and run it.
16	- **Doc-audit** reads a repo's history and lists which docs pages went stale and which shipped features have no docs.
17	
18	Every run and every audit ends with a receipt: what it cost, which plan tier caps it, and the proof it passed. cfo.ai models the prices and caps. neatlogs traces every run. Entire records the build.
19	
20	Success: a new visitor can say in one sentence what Doc-test does, what Doc-audit does, and why the result can be trusted, then try Doc-test.
21	
22	## Brand Personality
23	
24	Calm, precise, confident. Apple-like: light mode, real logos, dead simple, big type, one idea per screen, the fewest steps.
25	
26	## Anti-References
27	
28	- A page that reads like a log, a dashboard or a report. If a section needs the reader to decode it, it fails.
29	- Walls of text, long subtitles under headings, three claims in one paragraph.
30	- Mixing Doc-test and Doc-audit in the same section. Each gets its own section, its own background color, and its own proof.
31	- Identical card grids, hero-metric templates, gradient text, glassmorphism.
32	- Internal build trivia (trace ids, hashes, hackathon plumbing) on the main path.
33	
34	## Design Principles
35	
36	1. One section, one idea, one sentence of explanation.
37	2. Doc-test, Doc-audit and the receipt story each have a different background so a new reader always knows which tool they are reading about.
38	3. Show the thing, not a description of it: a real broken step, a real fix, a real receipt.
39	4. H2s are centered and have no subtitle. Links are always underlined. Content is centered unless a layout needs otherwise.
40	5. Real PRs, real repos, real logos beat claims.
41	
42	## Accessibility & Inclusion
43	
44	WCAG AA contrast. Honor `prefers-reduced-motion`. Never use color as the only signal. Underlined links. Works at 375 px wide with no sideways scroll.

86 7. Which docs did the product outgrow? Audit the whole docs set from the git history. 87 88 ```bash 89 firstrun audit fastapi/typer 90 ``` 91 92 ```bash 93 firstrun audit dbt-labs/dbt-core --docs-repo dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com 94 ``` 95 96 One blobless clone gives the whole history. The audit then works offline and costs $0 in model calls. Jev sorts commits with no conventional prefix when `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` is set, and every audit is one neatlogs trace. 97 98 - **Oldest first.** Every page, ranked by the date of its last edit. 99 - **Stale or quiet.** A page is stale when product commits on its topic landed after its last edit, and the report names those commits. An old page that nothing changed under is quiet, so the team can leave it alone. 100 - **Features with no docs.** Each user-facing commit in 120 days is checked against the docs text. A flag or name that no page mentions becomes a "Document this" card. 101 - **Proposal cards.** Document this, refresh this page, feature this, create content around a feature with 3 or more commits, and automate the release notes. 102 - **Drafts.** Release notes for the newest stable tag and up to 3 product highlights, written from commit subjects and pull request numbers. 103 104 `firstrun audit-issue` turns the newest audit into `issue.md`, one checkbox per card, and prints the `gh issue create` command. It opens nothing on its own. 105 106 To audit every week, copy [`examples/github-action/firstrun-audit.yml`](examples/github-action/firstrun-audit.yml) into `.github/workflows/`. Each Monday it audits the repo and updates one issue labeled `firstrun-audit`, so the docs team gets a fresh work list without anyone running a command. 107 108 `--docs-repo` reads the docs from a second repo when the docs site lives apart from the code. Inside this repo, each audit is published to `docs/audits/` and opens at [audit.html](https://1run.netlify.app/audit.html). 109 110

1	# FirstRun Business Plan
2	
3	FirstRun runs a dev tool's quickstart in a clean container every night, finds the first step that breaks, proves the fix with a second clean run, and drafts the docs PR. The buyer is a DevRel or docs team at a dev-tool company.
4	
5	The business plan sets the agent's spending limit. `firstrun econ` reads every neatlogs trace, cfo.ai turns the costs into a per-tier cap, and `firstrun run --tier` stops any run that spends past it.
6	
7	cfo.ai model, public and read-only: [https://cfo.ai/s/_u5lbrHIl9KX_JQE](https://cfo.ai/s/_u5lbrHIl9KX_JQE)
8	
9	## Three Tiers Price by Quickstarts Covered
10	
11	| Tier | Price per month | Quickstarts | Runs per month |
12	|---|---|---|---|
13	| Free | $0 | 1, weekly | 4 |
14	| Team | $49 | 10, nightly | 300 |
15	| Scale | $299 | 100, nightly, with PRs, Docs Bisect and Prerequisite Proof | 3,000 |
16	
17	## The Average Run Costs $0.0167, but One in Twenty Costs Three Times That
18	
19	neatlogs holds 64 `firstrun.run` traces from 2026-10-10. `firstrun econ` reads them and writes [`drivers.csv`](drivers.csv), the file cfo.ai imports. Each quantile row names the trace it came from, so a judge can open the trace behind any cost in the model.
20	
21	| Driver | Cost per run | neatlogs trace |
22	|---|---|---|
23	| Mean | $0.01672 | all 64 |
24	| p50 | $0.01076 | `cef9cc00bcc5369d74ffc7fc5f525244` |
25	| p90 | $0.04424 | `ec246a27f83c9e11d682eb09a1818f58` |
26	| p95 | $0.05078 | `9e30cd0f9cee66410c81fb3a34e03177` |
27	| Max | $0.10135 | `a462576e751e91543b5623185331d603` |
28	| Compute | $0.0019 | assumption: AWS t3.medium at $0.0416 an hour for the measured 164.8 s mean |
29	
30	The costs are Sonnet 5.5 list price, and Anthropic did not bill them. The 64 traces include 28 development runs, so the spread is wider than a production month would show.
31	
32	The expensive runs are the useful ones. A run that hits a broken step pays for recovery and for the second clean run. Of 19 real-world runs, 10 ended `verified` with 32 proven patches, and the 19 runs cost $0.97 in total. That is $0.0975 per verified quickstart (source: `runs/*/state.json`).
33	
34	## The Old $0.50 Cap Let a Scale Customer Cost Five Times the Price
35	
36	Before this plan, every run had the same cap of $0.50 in `src/firstrun/models.py`. That cap was 30 times the mean run cost, and nothing in the business set it.
37	
38	| Tier | Revenue per run | Margin at mean cost | Margin at p95 cost | Margin if every run hits $0.50 |
39	|---|---|---|---|---|
40	| Team | $0.1633 | 88.6% | 67.7% | -207.3% |
41	| Scale | $0.0997 | 81.3% | 47.1% | -403.6% |
42	
43	The mean says both tiers are healthy. The p95 says Scale falls below a 70% margin in a month with many broken quickstarts. The old cap says one bad month can cost a Scale customer's fee five times over.
44	
45	## The Margin Floor Sets the Cap, and the Agent Enforces It
46	
47	The founder picks one number, a 70% gross margin floor. The cap for each tier is the model spend one run may use and still keep that floor:
48	
49	```text
50	cap per run = price / runs per month x (1 - margin floor) - compute per run
51	```
52	
53	If every run in a month hits the cap, the tier still earns 70%. A Free run has no revenue, so its cap is the measured median run.
54	
55	| Tier | Cap per run | Measured runs over the cap |
56	|---|---|---|
57	| Free | $0.0108 | 48.4% |
58	| Team | $0.0471 | 7.8% |
59	| Scale | $0.0280 | 25.0% |
60	
61	`firstrun run <url> --tier scale` loads the cap from [`unit_economics.json`](unit_economics.json). The executor and the recovery agent both check it, and each check is a `budget` GUARDRAIL span in neatlogs. A run that passes the cap stops with `cost budget spent`, and the report names the step where it stopped.
62	
63	On the typer quickstart, `--tier scale` verified 7/7 steps at $0.0201. `--tier free` stopped at step 4 with `cost budget spent: $0.0115 of $0.0108`.
64	
65	The cap checks FirstRun's own cost count, which runs 39% above neatlogs on 43 matched runs ($1.5253 against $1.0989). So the cap stops a run early, never late.
66	
67	## Scale Needs a Fix, and the Data Names Two
68	
69	A 25% stop rate means Scale customers would see one run in four end early. The price or the allowance has to move. Both fixes come from the same formula.
70	
71	| Option | Price | Runs per month | Cap per run | Measured runs over the cap |
72	|---|---|---|---|---|
73	| Today | $299 | 3,000 | $0.0280 | 25.0% |
74	| Raise the price | $529 | 3,000 | $0.0510 | 4.7% |
75	| Halve the allowance | $299 | 1,500 (50 quickstarts) | $0.0579 | 3.1% |
76	
77	Team at $49 already stops only 7.8% of runs. A $53 price would cover the p95 run at the floor.
78	
79	## The Planner Fix From the Traces Cut Cost per Run by 24%
80	
81	neatlogs Detections and an Investigate run found the planner inventing steps. The fix shipped in commit 3ca6f11. The same 4 targets, before and after, as neatlogs measured them:
82	
83	| Agent | Model cost per run | Quickstarts finished | Failed steps recovered |
84	|---|---|---|---|
85	| v1 | $0.0262 | 2 of 4 | 0 |
86	| v2 | $0.0200 | 3 of 4 | 3 |
87	
88	## cfo.ai Shows the Old Cap Runs Out of Cash in Month 14
89	
90	Ari built the model in cfo.ai over MCP, in workspace "Atharva CFOAI", page "FirstRun model". Every formula reads its number from a "FirstRun drivers" table, and its "Driver source" column names the neatlogs trace behind each measured cost. The figures below were read back from cfo.ai, not computed by hand. Cost per run is $0.01862, the 64-trace mean plus compute. Gross margin includes Stripe fees.
91	
92	| Scenario | Scale gross margin | Team gross margin | Month 18 MRR | Month 18 cash |
93	|---|---|---|---|---|
94	| Base | 78.3% | 85.1% | $2,069 | $16,832 |
95	| Growth | 78.3% | 85.1% | $5,427 | $45,220 |
96	| Tail month: every run at p95 cost | 44.1% | 64.2% | $2,069 | $12,767 |
97	| Old cap: every Scale run at $0.50 | -406.6% | 85.1% | $2,069 | -$12,131 |
98	| Scale at $529 | 86.5% | 85.1% | $2,876 (Base plus the $807 Scale gain cfo.ai reported) | $21,293 |
99	| Scale at 1,500 runs | 87.7% | 85.1% | $2,069 | $17,390 |
100	
101	Under the old cap, cash first goes negative in December 2027, month 14. Every other Scenario has positive net cash flow, so cfo.ai shows no runway limit. Raising Scale to $529 earns the most cash. Halving the Scale allowance keeps the $299 price and still clears the 70% floor.
102	
103	## Both Scenarios Pay Back Fixed Costs in Month 2
104	
105	This hand-built table came before the cfo.ai model and uses the v1 cost of $0.02771 per run. The cfo.ai table above uses the 64-trace cost, so its month 18 cash is higher.
106	
107	Both scenarios start with $5,000 cash on 2026-11-01. Fixed costs are $25 a month. Monthly churn is 10% on Free, 5% on Team and 3% on Scale. Stripe takes 2.9% plus $0.30 per paid invoice.
108	
109	- **Base:** 10 new Free users a month. 1 new Team customer a month in months 2 to 6, then 2 a month. 1 new Scale customer in months 9, 12, 15 and 18.
110	- **Growth:** 30 new Free users a month. 3 new Team customers a month. 1 new Scale customer a month from month 4.
111	
112	| Scenario | Month | Free | Team | Scale | MRR | Costs | Cumulative cash |
113	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
114	| Base | 1 | 10.0 | 0.0 | 0.0 | $0 | $26 | $4,974 |
115	| Base | 6 | 46.9 | 4.5 | 0.0 | $222 | $76 | $5,377 |
116	| Base | 12 | 71.8 | 13.9 | 1.9 | $1,254 | $349 | $8,578 |
117	| Base | 18 | 85.0 | 20.8 | 3.5 | $2,069 | $566 | $15,747 |
118	| Growth | 1 | 30.0 | 3.0 | 0.0 | $147 | $58 | $5,089 |
119	| Growth | 6 | 140.6 | 15.9 | 2.9 | $1,649 | $468 | $8,268 |
120	| Growth | 12 | 215.3 | 27.6 | 8.0 | $3,741 | $1,062 | $20,757 |
121	| Growth | 18 | 255.0 | 36.2 | 12.2 | $5,428 | $1,542 | $41,180 |
122	
123	Customer counts are expected values, so they carry decimals. No salary is paid. With zero paying customers, $5,000 lasts about 190 months. One Team customer covers the $25 fixed costs. No customer has paid yet, so every customer count above is an assumption.
124	
125	## Rebuild the Model From the Traces
126	
127	1. Run `firstrun econ`. It reads neatlogs and rewrites `drivers.csv` and `unit_economics.json`.
128	2. Attach `drivers.csv` and `inputs.json` to Ari in cfo.ai, and paste the prompt below.
129	3. Run `firstrun run <url> --tier <name>`. The agent now spends inside the cap the plan set.
130	
131	```text
132	FirstRun is an AI agent that runs a dev tool's quickstart docs in a clean container every night and drafts a docs pull request when a step breaks. Customers are DevRel and docs teams at developer tool companies.
133	
134	Use the attached drivers.csv for every cost. Rows with measured=yes come from neatlogs traces, and the source column names the trace. Keep that source on each Variable. Rows with measured=no are assumptions, so label them as assumptions.
135	
136	Plans: Free at $0 (4 runs a month), Team at $49 (300 runs a month), Scale at $299 (3,000 runs a month). Cost per run is cost_per_run_mean plus compute_per_run. Add Stripe at 2.9% plus $0.30 per paid invoice, $25 fixed costs a month and no founder salary. Start with $5,000 cash on 2026-11-01 and model 18 months. Use the customer additions and churn rates in inputs.json for a Base and a Growth Scenario.
137	
138	Then make four more Scenarios from Base and compare them with Base on gross margin per plan, ending cash and runway:
139	1. "Tail month": cost per run is cost_per_run_p95 for every run.
140	2. "Old cap": cost per run is $0.50 for every Scale run, the cap before this plan.
141	3. "Scale at $529": Scale price $529, runs unchanged.
142	4. "Scale at 1,500 runs": Scale price $299, Scale runs 1,500.
143	
144	Show customers per plan, MRR, gross margin per plan, operating costs, ending cash and cash runway.

7	
8	# Grading Checklist and Judge Map
9	
10	Sources: `_agent-research/hackathon-rules-verbatim.md` for the rubric, `02 Judges and Mentors.md` for the people. The lead agent ticks this file at the end of every block. Atharva reads only the "Gaps" column. The audit of every row against the repo on Sunday 2026-10-11 is `37 Rubric Gap Audit Sun.md`.
11	
12	## Five Categories Carry 100 Points, and Each One Has a Proof File
13	
14	| Category | Weight | What earns it | Proof file or link | Owner | Status |
15	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
16	| The agent | 30% | All 8 focus areas visible in one run (table below) | `runs/*/report.md`, trace links | Lead | [ ] |
17	| neatlogs, Entire, cfo.ai | 25% | A clear role for each, covered in the video | `evidence/`, README sections | Lead | [ ] |
18	| Demo video | 20% | 3 minutes or less, 5 points for each tool | YouTube link | Vault chat | [ ] |
19	| Building in public | 15% | 5 or more posts tagged #neatHack, with failures and numbers | Post URLs in `hackathon.md` | Vault chat | [ ] |
20	| Usefulness and originality | 10% | A real docs team would run it nightly | README pitch, the PRs and issues opened | Lead | [ ] |
21	
22	## Eight Focus Areas Each Map to One Feature a Judge Can See
23	
24	| Focus area | FirstRun feature | Where the judge sees it |
25	|---|---|---|
26	| Planning | `planner` turns the docs page into a runbook | `runbook.json`, the `planner` span |
27	| Tool use | Firecrawl read, Docker run, Jev classify | One `TOOL` span per call |
28	| State | `state.json` after every step | `--resume` works after a forced crash |
29	| Context | Only the quickstart page and the pages a step needs | Token count per run in neatlogs |
30	| Execution | One fresh container per run | `step.<id>` spans with exit codes |
31	| Recovery | Classify, search, patch, retry, 3 attempts | A trace with a failed step and the retry |
32	| Verification | A model-free re-run in a new container | The `verify` span, status `verified` |
33	| Iteration | v1 traces, a detection, an Investigate, v2 traces | The before and after table |
34	
35	## Seven Claims Need Proof, and the Checklist Names the File
36	
37	- [ ] **Agent improved:** two neatlogs traces, v1 and v2, with the numbers table in the README. Real numbers only.
38	- [ ] **neatlogs used:** trace links in `evidence/neatlogs.md`, plus 2 detections, 1 Investigate and 1 eval.
39	- [ ] **Entire used:** `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer on every commit, the entire.io commit link with the full SHA, `evidence/graph.ndjson`, and the jury self-test output.
40	- [ ] **cfo.ai used:** the public cfo.ai share link and `BUSINESS_PLAN.md`, with price, costs, revenue and runway.
41	- [ ] **Recovery shown:** one exported failed-and-recovered trace in `evidence/`.
42	- [ ] **Built in public:** every post URL with #neatHack in `hackathon.md`.
43	- [ ] **Code written during the event:** the first commit is after 2026-10-10 12:30 IST, and `hackathon.md` says planning happened before in a private repo.
44	
45	## What Each Judge Will Look for, and the Artifact That Answers Them
46	
47	| Judge | Role | Looks for | Artifact that answers it |
48	|---|---|---|---|
49	| Haimantika Mitra | Docs at Entire | Entire on from commit 1. A README a developer can reproduce in minutes. | First commit carries a checkpoint. README has a 5-minute quickstart. |
50	| Abhi Singh | Solutions engineer at Entire | A clean install, real tests, cost numbers. | `pip install` then `firstrun run` works on a clean machine. `pytest` passes. Cost per run in the README. |
51	| Prateek Karnal | Parallel agents | Parallel work, measured numbers, an honest failure log. | The build used 5 parallel worker agents. The README carries a "what broke" section with numbers. |
52	| Ajay Yadav | neatlogs founder | A failure traced, fixed and proven fixed. A human asked only at the real call. | The ask-once store. A verified fix. No fully self-fixing loop. |
53	| Akshay Hangloo | neatlogs product | An agent that catches its own quality drop. Evals on real runs. A polished UI. | 2 detections, the AI evaluator, the static report page (T6). |
54	
55	## Five Mentors Add Questions, and Each One Gets a Short Answer Ready
56	
57	| Mentor | Probable question | Answer to have ready |
58	|---|---|---|
59	| Chetan Raj | Where does a judge stop trusting a demo? | The video shows a real run from terminal to trace, with no cuts inside the run. |
60	| Rohan Mukherjee | Can the agent game its own verification? | No. Verification calls no model and runs only the stored commands in a new container. |
61	| Rithvik K | What if the run crashes halfway? | `state.json` after each step and `--resume`. |
62	| Ankush Dharkar | What is the smallest human check? | One question, asked once, stored as a precedent. |
63	| Karan Pargal | What do the first 30 seconds show? | One broken step in red, then the agent finding it. |
64	
65	## The Community Award Looks at Genuine Interest, so Three Things Count
66	
67	1. **Quality of the launch.** One post a day with a failure and a number in it.
68	2. **Gifts to the judges' own products.** An issue or a PR for neatlogs and Entire, opened by hand, then a thank-you post.
69	3. **Replies to every comment in the first 24 hours.** Never buy likes. Bots disqualify the entry.
70	
71	## Seven Gaps Lose Points Quietly, so the Lead Checks Them Every Night
72	
73	1. A tool with no use that day (rule F5).
74	2. A video beat that names fewer than 5 points for a tool.
75	3. A post with no number or no failure in it.
76	4. A trace link that needs a login. Check logged out.
77	5. A commit with no `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer.
78	6. A cfo.ai number that did not come from neatlogs.
79	7. A claim in the README with no proof file.
80	
81	## Submit Between 7:00 and 7:05 PM on Monday
82	
83	The F4 controls live in `07 Rules We Follow.md`. This file adds one check: before clicking, tick all seven claims above. If one is open, submit anyway, and finish it before 11:55 PM in the repo.

+## Two Launched Evals Scored 67 Traces and Found Where the Agent Overclaims
+
+Atharva launched both evals from the dashboard on 2026-10-11, with the AI judge as the only reviewer. Both finished at 100%. The scores come from `neatlogs evals responses`.
+
+**FirstRun run review** (`15b7ef6b`) judged 52 real runs, tagged `radar`, `real`, `real2`, `v1` and `v2`.
+
+| Question | Result |
+|---|---|
+| Reported first failed step is the real one | 46 of 52 |
+| Run's failure class matches the container output | 38 of 52 |
+| Every patch backed by a passing verify rerun | 34 of 52 |
+| Overall score, 1 to 5 | mean 3.69. 23 runs scored 5, 17 scored 1 or 2 |
+
+The judge's own failure classes were environment 28, none 12, docs bug 9 and needs secret 3.
+
+The 17 low scores show 3 patterns:
+
+1. Runs that stopped before a clean rerun get no proof. Five Dagster runs stopped after `create-dagster: command not found` and `no such option: --group`. Flask and Litestar server steps timed out with exit 124, before the server-step fix landed.
+2. A missing API key counted as a docs bug. Two runs that failed with `No API key provided` reported `docs_bug`, and the judge said `needs_secret`.
+3. One run stopped at `read_docs` with `Insufficient credits`, so it had no steps to judge.
+
+**FirstRun audit review** (`14dfda88`) judged the 15 newest audits.
+
+| Question | Result |
+|---|---|
+| Root summary matches the page and feature outputs | 14 of 15 |
+| Every evidence card cites a commit or PR | 15 of 15 |
+| Stale pages whose commits do not fit the topic | 0 in all 15 |
+| Overall score, 1 to 5 | mean 4.87. 14 audits scored 5 |
+
+**The detection behind the runs.** "docs step broke" flagged 78 tool spans, all on Oct 10 and 11, from a baseline of 0. [Screenshot](nl-detection-docs-step-broke.png).
+
 **A radar batch for the evaluations to judge.** `scripts/radar.py` ranked 70 Exa results with Jev, and FirstRun ran the top 18 official quickstarts in 3 parallel lanes, tagged `radar`, under the Team cost cap. Two runs exposed a FirstRun bug: a dev server step (`flask --app hello run`, `litestar run`) never exits, so it timed out. The fix passes a server step once its output says it listens. The `radar-v2` rerun took Flask from 0 of 4 steps to verified 4 of 4.
 
 ## The Integration Check Passed the Organizer's Gates

25%neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai

neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai Each Did One Job

  • neatlogs

    Traces every run, and found the agent's own bug.

    • Each run is one firstrun.run trace with WORKFLOW, AGENT, TOOL and GUARDRAIL spans. neatlogs.md
    • 2 detections run on every trace. "Planner invented a step" flagged 3 v1 planner spans. "Docs step broke" flagged 78 tool spans. Detection screenshot
    • Investigate traced the invented steps to the planner prompt. A Claude Code session read the detection over the neatlogs MCP server and shipped the fix. Investigate result Commit 3ca6f11
    • 2 AI evaluators scored real traces. The run judge named the real failed step in 46 of 52 runs and scored 17 runs at 1 or 2. The audit judge averaged 4.87 of 5 over 15 audits. Eval scores
    • Cost per run fell from $0.0262 to $0.0200, as neatlogs measured it. Before and after
    • neatlogs trace pages need a login. The trace IDs are in neatlogs.md, and one full trace is exported to the repo.

  • Entire

    Recorded the session behind each agent commit, and reviewed every layer.

    • 74 of 88 normal commits carry an Entire-Checkpoint: trailer, counted with git log on 2026-10-11. entire.md
    • The planner fix commit opens its whole session with no login, checkpoint 01M4JGJ6NTE7YNB9Z0YW5FYVHN. Entire commit page
    • Trails 3 to 12 cover every commit since kickoff. The runners found 3 real bugs, and all 3 are fixed. Trail findings
    • The build agents searched the repo through Entire Graph: 10 calls saved about 56,254 tokens. graph.ndjson
    • The Entire judge plugin scored the repo 3.93 of 5, with integrity 5.0 and no excluded work. Jury self-test
    • Trail pages need an entire.io login. The 4 setup commits before the first agent session and 10 site commits carry no trailer. The self-test ran at 42 commits and flags thin commit-to-session coverage.

  • cfo.ai

    Turned the measured cost into a price and a cost cap per plan.

    • Ari built the model over the cfo.ai MCP server. It is public and read-only. cfo.ai model
    • Every cost comes from neatlogs. The drivers file holds 88 traces, and each cost row names its trace. drivers.csv
    • A 70% margin floor sets the cap per run: Free $0.0135, Team $0.0470, Scale $0.0279. Plan page
    • Under the old fixed $0.50 cap, cash goes negative in month 14. BUSINESS_PLAN.md
    • A live run on the Free cap stopped at step 4 with cost budget spent. Pull request 15
    • The tables inside BUSINESS_PLAN.md use the earlier 64-trace data. The caps above come from the 88-trace refresh in drivers.csv.

10%Usefulness and originality

FirstRun Found 4 Real Docs Bugs and Sent 4 Upstream PRs

  • dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com #10149 OpenFix the jafgen command in the DuckDB quickstart

    jafgen --years 6 fails. Docs Bisect found the release that dropped the flag in 5 probes.

  • dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com #10150 OpenState the Python version the DuckDB quickstart needs

    The repo pins networkx 3.7, which needs Python 3.12. The guide named no version.

  • entireio/cli #2724 OpenSay where install.sh puts entire on Linux

    After a clean install, entire is not on PATH.

  • accuknox/help #671 OpenPoint knoxctl at the latest release and list the APT prerequisites

    The page named 0.9.0 as latest while the installer fetched 0.9.58.

  • Read the bisect comment on #10149: jafgen 0.3.1 passes, 0.4.6 fails, $0 in model calls.
  • Open the dbt-core Doc-audit board: 7 repos audited, 102 stale pages found.
  • Open an audit receipt: every run and every audit ends with one.

Seven Claims, Each With the File That Proves It

  1. The agent improved.before_after_traces.json8 neatlogs traces, 4 before the fix and 4 after. Cost is list price, not billed.
  2. neatlogs was used.evidence/neatlogs.mdTrace pages need a neatlogs login. The IDs and one exported trace are in the repo.
  3. Entire was used.evidence/entire.md74 of 88 normal commits carry a checkpoint trailer, not all of them. Merge commits carry none by design.
  4. cfo.ai was used.The public cfo.ai modelOpens with no login. The plan and every assumption are in business/BUSINESS_PLAN.md.
  5. Recovery is shown.trace-recovered-entire-v2.mdThe trace status reads ERROR because a failed step rolls up to the trace. The run itself ended verified.
  6. The build happened in public.The Built in Public table11 of 13 published posts carry #neatHack.
  7. The code was written during the event.First commit 96541a82026-10-10 at 12:34 IST, 4 minutes after the 12:30 kickoff. Planning happened before, in a private repo.

Five Things Broke While Building, and Each One Has a Number

  1. 206 s

    Git 2.33 hung the Entire post-commit hook, and one checkpoint was lost. Git 2.55.0 fixed it, and the next hook took 3 s.

  2. 3

    The first live run split into 3 neatlogs traces. The CLI now opens one firstrun.run trace around the whole run.

  3. 50

    Each pytest run exported about 50 empty traces. The test fixture now sets an empty key, and the next run exported 0.

  4. 39%

    FirstRun counts cost 39% above neatlogs: $1.5253 against $1.0989 on 43 runs. The cap uses the higher count, so it stops a run early, never late.

  5. 2

    On Dagster, FirstRun called 2 gaps docs bugs, but the page already covered both. No PR went out, and every PR draft now gets a source check.

What Broke While Building in the README, and the known limits

Two Commands Install FirstRun and Run a Quickstart

Install and run
$ pip install git+https://github.com/HighnessAtharva/firstrun
$ firstrun https://docs.example.com/quickstart

A run needs Python 3.11 or newer, Git, Docker and a Claude token in CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN. README quickstart

Run the offline tests, no network, Docker or keys
$ git clone https://github.com/HighnessAtharva/firstrun
$ cd firstrun && pip install -e ".[dev]" && pytest -q

CI on main on 2026-10-11 passed 295 tests. It skipped 59 that need FIRSTRUN_LIVE=1 or a human check, and 1 is an expected failure. GitHub Actions

Seven Claims, Each With the File That Proves It

  1. The agent improved.before_after_traces.json8 neatlogs traces, 4 before the fix and 4 after. Cost is list price, not billed.
  2. neatlogs was used.evidence/neatlogs.mdTrace pages need a neatlogs login. The IDs and one exported trace are in the repo.
  3. Entire was used.evidence/entire.md74 of 88 normal commits carry a checkpoint trailer, not all of them. Merge commits carry none by design.
  4. cfo.ai was used.The public cfo.ai modelOpens with no login. The plan and every assumption are in business/BUSINESS_PLAN.md.

  7. The code was written during the event.First commit 96541a82026-10-10 at 12:34 IST, 4 minutes after the 12:30 kickoff. Planning happened before, in a private repo.

Five Things Broke While Building, and Each One Has a Number

  1. 206 s

    Git 2.33 hung the Entire post-commit hook, and one checkpoint was lost. Git 2.55.0 fixed it, and the next hook took 3 s.

  2. 3

    The first live run split into 3 neatlogs traces. The CLI now opens one firstrun.run trace around the whole run.

  3. 50

    Each pytest run exported about 50 empty traces. The test fixture now sets an empty key, and the next run exported 0.

  4. 39%

    FirstRun counts cost 39% above neatlogs: $1.5253 against $1.0989 on 43 runs. The cap uses the higher count, so it stops a run early, never late.

  5. 2

    On Dagster, FirstRun called 2 gaps docs bugs, but the page already covered both. No PR went out, and every PR draft now gets a source check.

What Broke While Building in the README, and the known limits

Two Commands Install FirstRun and Run a Quickstart

Install and run
$ pip install git+https://github.com/HighnessAtharva/firstrun
$ firstrun https://docs.example.com/quickstart

A run needs Python 3.11 or newer, Git, Docker and a Claude token in CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN. README quickstart

Run the offline tests, no network, Docker or keys
$ git clone https://github.com/HighnessAtharva/firstrun
$ cd firstrun && pip install -e ".[dev]" && pytest -q

CI on main on 2026-10-11 passed 295 tests. It skipped 59 that need FIRSTRUN_LIVE=1 or a human check, and 1 is an expected failure. GitHub Actions

content.text:
I built the For Judges page and committed it as `01fa514` on branch `worktree-agent-af89594989dfade04`. Nothing is pushed, and no PR is open. The commit has no `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer, because I stopped its stuck `prepare-commit-msg` hook (PID 18344, the one for this worktree) as you said.

**Base change:** The worktree started at `ccbfed1`, which did not have PRODUCT.md or the new homepage. Those were on `feat/audit-receipt`. `origin/main` (`8f19e18`) contains that branch plus newer neatlogs eval scores, so I fast-forwarded to `origin/main`. The branch had no commits of its own, so nothing was lost.

**Files changed**
- `docs/judges/index.html` is the new page. All CSS is inline, and the only JS is the copy button.
- `docs/index.html` gets one footer link, "For judges".
- `docs/assets/site-nav.js` gets a "For judges" nav link, marked as the current page on this page. On phones it appears in the burger menu. I also fixed the mobile menu text: Plan and For judges now say "Its own page", not "On the home page". The nav fits at 1280, 880 and 862 px. Below 860 px the links move into the burger menu as before.

**Sections, in order**
1. **Hero:** four large numbered links (demo, AccuKnox receipt, before and after table, recovered trace). Below them is a bar of the 5 rubric categories, each width set by its weight, each linking to its section.
2. **The agent (30%):** the 8 focus areas, each with a GitHub link to the code line and its span. Then the ask-once rule (below 0.7 confidence, stored in `precedents.json`) and the v1 vs v2 table. I recomputed every table value from `before_after_traces.json`, and they match.
3. **neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai (25%):** one block per tool, each with its role, its proof and a caveat line.
4. **Demo (20%):** the thumbnail and the YouTube link, 2:59.
5. **Building in public (15%):** the 11 tagged posts from hackathon.md (10 on X, 1 on LinkedIn).
6. **Usefulness (10%):** the 4 PRs (all open), the bisect comment, the dbt-core Doc-audit board and an audit receipt.
7. **Seven claims:** each claim with one link and one honest note. The first commit is `96541a8` at 2026-10-10 12:34:51 IST.
8. **What broke:** 5 items, each led by a number: 206 s, 3, 50, 39%, 2.
9. **Reproduce:** the README install and run commands and the test commands, each with a copy button.
10. **Footer:** a link back to the homepage.

**Checks**
- I took screenshots at 1280 and 768 px, and at 375 px through an iframe. At 375 px the page has no sideways scroll.
- The copy button works, and the console shows no errors.
- No em or en dashes are on the page.
- The test suite on this commit gives 314 passed, 64 skipped and 1 expected failure. The README badge records 295 from CI on 2026-10-11. The page now gives both numbers, because a judge who runs the suite will see 314.

**External links checked logged out (HTTP status)**

| Link | Status |
|---|---|
| YouTube `JJNWWhSV9pc` | 200. oEmbed confirms the title "Your Docs Lie. FirstRun DocTest Proves It" |
| `cfo.ai/s/_u5lbrHIl9KX_JQE` | 200 |
| Entire commit page for `3ca6f118…` | 200 |
| Entire session `ae05fb29…` | 200, checked but not used on the page |
| Entire Trail 3 | 200, but it redirects to the login page |
| dbt #10149, dbt #10150, entireio/cli #2724, accuknox/help #671 | 200. The GitHub API says all 4 are open |
| firstrun PR #15 | 200. The API says merged |
| Bisect comment `6096827074` | 200 |
| GitHub commits `96541a8`, `0a00fbf`, `3ca6f11` | 200 |
| GitHub Actions page | 200 |
| `firstrun.atharvashah.com` | 200 |
| `neatlogs.com/hackathon` | 200 |
| LinkedIn post | 200, and the page carries #neatHack |
| 12 X posts | 200 on oEmbed and on x.com |

A script checked every GitHub blob path, line anchor and heading anchor against the repo files, and all of them resolve.

**Left out**
- **Two untagged posts:** the Sat 19:11 and Sun 10:32 X posts. The page points to the full table in hackathon.md instead.
- **The Entire session link:** I did not use the session URL from `evidence/README.md`, because the commit page already proves the same claim.
- **neatlogs trace links:** no trace is public, so the page names only trace IDs and the exported trace file.

**What a judge still cannot check**
- **neatlogs trace pages need a login.** The page says so, and it points to the exported trace and the trace IDs.
- **Entire Trail pages need a login.** The page says so.
- **Four posts may look untagged:** Sat 15:15, 18:15, 21:15 and Sun 07:32. The public X preview and the X syndication endpoint (cdn.syndication.twimg.com) both cut the text before the tag. Only hackathon.md says they carry #neatHack. A judge must click "Show more" on X to see the tag.
- **Business plan numbers:** The tables inside `BUSINESS_PLAN.md` still use the older 64-trace data. The caps on the page come from the 88-trace refresh in `drivers.csv`. The page states this caveat.
- **Checkpoint coverage:** 14 normal commits carry no checkpoint trailer. The jury self-test ran at 42 commits and says commit-to-session coverage is thin. Both caveats are on the page.
